quiz.q: The atomization energy of H₂SO₄ is about 600 kcal/mol. An error of 6 kcal/mol is therefore about…
quiz.explain: 6/600 = 1 %. Large reaction energies can carry large absolute errors even when the relative error looks small, and chemistry is decided by absolute energies.

quiz.q: Which species in this experiment are **open-shell** (unpaired electrons)?
options: The O and S atoms (triplets), the H atom (doublet) and O₂ (triplet)
quiz.explain: Atoms with partly filled p shells are high-spin in their ground state, and O₂ is the classic triplet molecule. Running them as singlets gives a converged, perfectly wrong energy.

quiz.q: Ozone (O₃) is notoriously difficult for DFT. Why?
options: It is too large for def2-TZVP
Its electronic structure has significant multireference (static-correlation) character
quiz.explain: Ozone's ground state is not well described by a single Slater determinant (it has partial diradical character). Single-determinant Kohn–Sham DFT with approximate functionals struggles with such systems.

quiz.q: CaO is part of the database MN15 was fitted to. What does that mean for MN15's result on reaction 5b?
options: It is an independent test of MN15
MN15's parameters were adjusted (among many other data) to reproduce this value, so good agreement is expected, not impressive
MN15 cannot be used for CaO
The reference value was computed with MN15
quiz.explain: Training-set data are not a fair test. To judge a functional, look at systems it was not fitted to.
